Endocrinology · published research

Pancreatic beta-cell regeneration

One cell-culture study found increased pancreatic beta-cell replication and cell-cycle progression after red-light exposure. Animal and human regeneration outcomes have not been reported in this exact category.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One cell-culture study found increased pancreatic beta-cell replication and cell-cycle progression after red-light exposure. Animal and human regeneration outcomes have not been reported in this exact category.

Summary of the Evidence

One exact-category primary publication examines pancreatic beta-cell regeneration. It is an in-vitro experiment using cultured cells, not a clinical trial or an animal study. Broader diabetes and islet publications were not counted as direct beta-cell regeneration evidence because their main outcomes do not establish regeneration in this specific category. No independent replication is identified in the database.

Human and clinical evidence

No human study directly testing PBM for pancreatic beta-cell regeneration was identified. The available publication does not report restoration of insulin-producing cell mass in people or a clinical diabetes outcome.

Animal evidence

No animal experiment directly testing regeneration of pancreatic beta cells was identified in this exact category. Related diabetes-model findings are not equivalent to demonstrating that new functional beta cells formed.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Huang and colleagues found that low-intensity laser irradiation increased replication and cell-cycle progression in cultured pancreatic beta cells. Pharmacologic activation and inhibition experiments implicated an Akt1/GSK3β signaling pathway in the response. The study reports a cellular proliferation outcome; it does not demonstrate that the new cells matured, secreted insulin appropriately, or improved glucose regulation in an organism (Huang et al. 2015).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The experiment used 633-nm red visible light at 10 mW/cm² and tested fluences of 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, and 1.2 J/cm². The database record describes a dose-response experiment, but one cell model cannot identify a treatment regimen for an intact pancreas. The study did not compare light-delivery routes through tissue or test long-term cell behavior.

Interpretation

The reported increase in beta-cell replication is a direct laboratory result and provides a specific mechanism for further testing. It remains an in-vitro finding. Whether PBM can safely increase functional beta-cell mass, preserve insulin release, or improve diabetes outcomes has not been shown.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for in-vitro beta-cell proliferation
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One cultured-cell study found increased beta-cell replication and cell-cycle progression and linked the response to Akt1 and GSK3β signaling. The result is biologically specific but has not been repeated in another cell model or tested in an intact pancreas. Replication with functional insulin-release and safety measures, followed by animal studies, would be needed to support a broader regenerative claim.
